title: What Is a Customs Clearance Delay and How Do You Fix It?
summary: Customs clearance delays can hold up shipments and add unexpected costs. Learn why they happen, how long they usually take, and how to prevent them.

A customs clearance delay means your shipment is being held at the border while customs authorities review, correct, or collect something before they release it. It is not a seizure or a penalty, and your goods are not lost.


Most of these delays trace back to a short list of fixable problems:


- incomplete paperwork
- the wrong HTS code
- unpaid duties
- security, safety, or regulatory screening
- port congestion


The frustrating part is that most sellers can’t immediately understand the root cause of why this has happened. Instead, they see symptoms like a shipment stuck in customs, an unexpected demurrage bill, or a customer complaining that they haven’t yet received their order.


This guide covers what causes customs clearance delays, how long they last, what they cost you, and how to prevent them at scale.


## What Is a Customs Clearance Delay?


A customs clearance delay is when customs authorities pause the release of a shipment because the entry is incomplete, unclear, or flagged for review.


Customs clearance is the process every cross-border shipment goes through at the border. The customs office reviews your documentation, checks the country of origin, assesses[tariffs and taxes](https://www.getsphere.com/blog/tariff-vs-tax) , and decides whether the goods can enter the country. When that process stalls, your shipment sits in limbo.


This process can be confusing and stressful for sellers. Here is what a clearance delay is not:


- It is not a seizure. Seizure is a separate and much more serious outcome tied to a compliance violation.
- It is not a penalty. Penalties are assessed separately and can apply even after your goods are released.
- It is not a refusal. Your shipment has simply not been released yet.


In the US, the clock starts the moment the shipment lands.[Entry documents](https://www.cbp.gov/sites/default/files/assets/documents/2020-Feb/icp073_3_0.pdf) have to be filed within 15 calendar days of arrival at a port of entry. If nobody files, the goods move to a general order warehouse and the importer of record starts paying storage. Once entry documents are filed, CBP has 5 working days from presentation to decide whether to release, detain, or seize the merchandise.


## What Causes Customs Clearance Delays?


Most customs clearance delays come from five causes:


- bad paperwork
- an incorrect tariff code
- unpaid duties
- regulatory screening
- port congestion


Four of the five of these common factors are within your control.


### Inaccurate or Incomplete Paperwork


Incomplete paperwork is one of the most common causes of clearance delays. Missing addresses, vague product descriptions, a declared value that does not match the commercial invoice, or a packing list with weights that do not line up with the container will all trigger a review.


Customs authorities are not guessing at what is in your box. They are matching your documents against each other. When "assorted electronics" appears where a specific product description belongs, or when a certificate of origin is a missing document in the file, somebody has to stop and determine the reason for the discrepancy.


Unfortunately, you don’t receive a handy report with the reason why your shipment is stuck in customs. Instead, you and your customs broker must play detective to determine the problem and attempt to fix it.


### HS/Tariff Code Misclassification


An incorrect[HS or HTS code](https://www.getsphere.com/blog/what-is-import-tax) triggers review when it does not match your product description or when the duty rate looks inconsistent with the declared value. Customs officers see these mismatches every day and they are trained to pull them.


Misclassification is also a direct penalty risk, which makes it different from most other delay causes. The hold and the fine are two separate problems, and you can end up with both from the same code.


### Unpaid or Disputed Duties and Taxes


Customs will not release a shipment until the required duties,[import taxes](https://www.getsphere.com/blog/what-is-import-tax) , and fees are paid. That sounds obvious, but the payment request could go to an old email address, land in spam, or reach your buyer who was not expecting a bill and writes to you for support. Meanwhile, the shipment sits in customs clearance delay while no one is aware payment is due.


### Security, Safety, and Regulatory Screening


Some shipments get flagged for reasons that have nothing to do with your paperwork quality. Prohibited items, hazardous materials, and goods that require special permits all draw closer inspection.


Other agencies can hold your goods too, even after customs is satisfied. Food imports may need FDA sign-off. Agricultural products may need USDA clearance. Until the relevant agency signs off, the shipment does not move out of customs clearance.


### Port Congestion


During peak shipping seasons, processing slows across the board no matter how clean your entry is. This is the one cause for delay you cannot fix even with the most pristine documentation. Build a buffer into your lead times during peak season and you (and your customers) will feel the pain less.


## How Long Does a Customs Clearance Delay Last?


If your documentation and classification are correct and filed in advance, your shipment can actually clear customs before your cargo even arrives. Experienced freight forwarders routinely clear cargo several days ahead of arrival as standard practice, which removes the wait entirely.


Once a shipment is actually flagged for one of the customs inspections, the exam type sets the timeline:


Inspection type


What happens


Typical duration


Non-intrusive (VACIS) exam


Container is X-rayed or gamma scanned without being opened


1 to 2 days


Tail gate exam


Container doors are opened and contents are visually checked


3 to 5 days


Intensive exam


Container is moved to a facility and fully unloaded for inspection


5 to 7 days, longer if the site is backed up


The pattern here matters more than the specific numbers. Everything that prevents a delay happens before the shipment leaves. Once it is flagged, the inspection type sets the minimum expected time and there is very little you or your courier can do to speed it up.


## What Does a Customs Clearance Delay Cost?


A customs clearance delay costs you in three ways: storage fees that accumulate daily, penalties tied to the underlying paperwork error, and damage to the customer relationship.


### Demurrage and Detention Fees


Most ports allow approximately 2 to 7 free days before charges start. After that, demurrage–the charge for staying in port past the grace period–typically runs approximately $75 to $300 per container per day, depending on the port and the carrier.


Note that the cost is per container. The cost for a five-day hold on a handful of containers accumulates quickly.


### Misclassification Penalties


Penalties for misclassification are separate from the delay and can apply even after your goods are released. Under 19 USC 1592, US Customs and Border Protection scales civil penalties based on their determination of your level of negligence.


When there is no lost duty revenue, the[statutory maximums](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-19/chapter-I/part-171/appendix-Appendix%20B%20to%20Part%20171) are 20% of the dutiable value for negligence, 40% for gross negligence, and up to the full domestic value of the merchandise for fraud. CBP's own mitigation guidelines land most settled cases lower: approximately 5% to 20% of dutiable value for negligence, 25% to 40% for gross negligence, and 50% to 80% for outright fraud.


### Knock-On Costs for E-Commerce Sellers


For e-commerce sellers, a customs delay can also damage your customer relationship. A held shipment means a missed delivery promise, a customer holding an unexpected duties bill, support tickets, and refund requests.


## How to Avoid Customs Clearance Delays


You avoid customs clearance delays by getting these five things right before the shipment departs:


- File a complete, accurate commercial invoice and packing list. Correct declared value, detailed product descriptions, matching addresses, and consistent weights.
- Classify every product under the correct HS or HTS code up front. This is both a top delay cause and a direct penalty risk, so it earns the attention twice over.
- Pre-pay duties and taxes rather than leaving them to be settled at the border. This is effectively what DDP does.
- File paperwork with customs in advance of arrival instead of waiting for the shipment to land. Advance filing through[CBP's Automated Commercial Environment](https://www.cbp.gov/trade/automated) is what lets cargo clear customs before it docks.
- Confirm regulatory permits are secured before the goods ship, if your product category needs them. FDA and USDA sign-offs cannot be rushed once the shipment is already sitting.


## DDP vs DDU — Which Reduces Clearance Risk?


Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) means the seller pays duties and taxes upfront. Delivered Duty Unpaid (DDU) means the buyer pays duties and taxes upon arrival of the shipment. (DDU is now often referred to as DAP or Delivered at Place).


DDP reduces clearance delay risk when you are selling direct to consumers. DDU shifts that risk to the buyer, which works better when the buyer is a business that imports regularly but less well when that buyer is a consumer who may not be expecting to pay an additional fee.


If you sell direct to consumers across borders, DDP generally reduces both delay risk and surprise-fee friction. If your buyer is a business used to acting as its own importer of record, DDU is more common and the delay risk sits with them.


## Customs Clearance Delays at Scale: The E-Commerce Problem


At scale, a customs clearance delay can become a huge business liability.


### Why Scale Changes the Risk


One misclassified SKU in a mixed shipment can hold up the entire shipment, not just that item. A single bad code on a low-value product can strand everything traveling with it.


Manual classification does not scale cleanly either. A person or team reviewing each SKU against tariff schedules works fine for a small catalog going to two countries. It breaks down across a large, changing catalog and a dozen destination markets. Tariff schedules also shift over time, and keeping up with those changes by hand is where most teams fall behind.


### Classification Debt


Classification debt occurs when your business’s classifications do not change with the times.


A catalog gets classified correctly at launch. Then SKUs get added, product lines change, and tariff schedules change. The delays show up months or years later, while the team assumes they are[handling customs correctly](https://www.getsphere.com/blog/customs-compliance) .

Sphere keeps a human checkpoint in the process. AI classifies at scale, then your team or Sphere's tax team signs off before your business relies on the data. This middle ground keeps your business protected and up-to-date when it comes to cross-border shipping and customs.


A customs clearance delay is a hold, not a final judgment. Your shipment has not been seized, and in most cases the fix is a specific document, a payment, or a corrected code.


The catch is that almost every fix is retroactive once the shipment is already at the border. Accurate paperwork, correct HTS codes, pre-paid duties, and advance filing are what keep goods moving. At scale, that means treating classification as something you constantly maintain rather than something you set and forget.


If a shipment is stuck in customs right now, call your customs broker or freight forwarder and find out exactly what is holding it. If you want to stop having this conversation altogether, fix the classification layer first.
